# job: # The per-job scoring projection NOTES-authoring.md 4.5.4 describes. A recording
# is what the baseline did and stays whole; this file is what the *scorer* is
# allowed to compare, per job, and why.
# Rules:
#   head:N          keep the first N lines, discard the rest
#   drop:<regex>    discard every line the (unanchored, re.search) pattern hits
#   sort            sort each maximal run of lines starting with "|", which is
#                   a show() grid's data rows; the header is a run of one, so
#                   it does not move. Gives up row order, nothing else
#   cut:A;;B        drop the block from the first line matching A up to the
#                   next line matching B, which is kept; repeatable, runs to
#                   EOF if B never matches
#   vec             canonicalize a show() grid -- drop the +---+ rules, rstrip
#                   every cell -- and rewrite a cell that is a bracketed list of
#                   numbers as [<vec:N>], N being the element count, or
#                   [<vec:...>] where show() truncated the cell. Names, row
#                   order, row count, every string cell and the printed arity
#                   still compare; only the float values stop comparing.
# Classes. There are two reasons a line cannot be compared as text, they are not
# the same reason, and the file used to have only the first:
#   RUN   the line moves between two runs of the *same* build. The job must
#         therefore also be declared ORDER or VALUE in build/determinism.tsv,
#         which is the file that says what a recording may be compared as
#         within a rung.
#   RUNG  the line is perfectly repeatable within a rung -- determinism.tsv
#         says STABLE and means it -- and moves between Spark versions for a
#         mechanism no migration guide documents. Rule 5 lets a step re-record
#         an input only when the target version documents the change, so an
#         undocumented cross-version move can be neither scored as text nor
#         made must-flip. It is projected instead, and the job must be STABLE
#         in determinism.tsv, not loose.
# The distinction is load-bearing and was got wrong first: the tempting fix for
# the two RUNG rows below was to relabel them VALUE in determinism.tsv so that
# the old one-way cross-check would pass. That would have been a false statement
# about within-run repeatability, made to satisfy a bookkeeping invariant, and
# it would have silently licensed every later step to stop comparing those jobs
# as text within a rung. projection.py --selftest now asserts the classes
# separately: RUN rows and the ORDER/VALUE declarations must name exactly the
# same jobs, and every RUNG row must name a job declared STABLE.
# Every row is a line of the baseline's behavior this suite has given up on
# measuring, so each one carries the mechanism, named in source or in an
# upstream library. "Looked flaky once" is not a mechanism: rule 7's "record
# every candidate twice" is the floor for admitting a row here, not the
# standard. Twenty rows, and twenty is meant to be the whole list.
# A RUNG row costs more than a RUN row and the cost is easy to miss: the
# projection is one file shipped to all ten steps, so a job projected for a
# mechanism that lands at rung 7 stops being compared at rungs 1-6 as well,
# where it was byte-exact. That is why `vec` was built instead of reusing
# `drop`: the cheap line-class rule drop:^[+|] would have reconciled the same
# five jobs while keeping 11, 18, 5, 15 and 14 of their 40, 47, 73, 44 and 35
# lines, throwing away whole neighbouring tables that never moved. `vec` keeps
